'''''Iris florentina''''', also known as '''''Iris''''' '''''albicans''''', '''cemetery iris''', '''white cemetery iris''', or the '''white flag iris''', is a species of [[Iris (plant)|iris]] which was planted on graves in Muslim regions and grows in many countries throughout the Middle East and northern Africa. It was later introduced to Spain, and then other European countries.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Iris Species Database<!-- Bot generated title --> |url=http://www.badbear.com/signa/signa.pl?Iris-albicans |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303182949/http://www.badbear.com/signa/signa.pl?Iris-albicans |archive-date=2016-03-03 |access-date=2007-02-18}}</ref>

The identity of the plant first described by [[Carl Linnaeus]] as ''Iris florentina'' remains unclear, {{as of|2021|December|lc=yes}}. In [[horticulture]], it has been treated as a white-flowered variant of [[Iris × germanica|''Iris'' × ''germanica'']], under names such as ''Iris germanica'' nothovar. ''florentina'', ''Iris'' × ''germanica'' var. ''florentina'' and ''Iris'' × ''germanica'' 'Florentina'. ''Iris florentina'' has also been treated as the correct name for the true species also known as ''Iris albicans'' <small>Lange</small>.

It is cultivated as an ornamental plant in [[temperateness|temperate]] regions almost worldwide and is a [[rhizomatous]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] from southern [[Europe]], mainly [[Italy]] (including the city of [[Florence]]) and [[France]]. It has a thick violet-scented rhizome, sword-like green or grey-green semi-evergreen leaves, a tall branched stem, and many flowers that are white and tinged or flushed with blue, pale blue, or lavender in spring or summer, and a white and yellow beard. It is also grown to produce [[orris-root]], a scented substance used in perfumes, soaps, tooth cleanser, and clothes washing powder. Medicinally it was used as an expectorant and decongestant. It is made from the rhizomes of ''Iris florentina'', ''[[Iris germanica]]'' and ''[[Iris pallida]]''. The flower is commonly attributed with the [[fleur-de-lis]].

==Description==
[[File:Iris florentina flower.jpg|thumb|Iris florentina flower in late April.]]
[[File:Irisflorentina ap.jpg|thumb]]
''Iris florentina'' has a thick or stout rhizome, which is short, fleshy, horizontal, and has a strong violet scent.<ref name=ruth>Ruth D. Wrensch {{Google books|6N8koMi28mgC|The Essence of Herbs|page=213}}</ref><ref name=centrechem>{{cite web |title=Iris florentina |url=http://www.centerchem.com/Products/DownloadFile.aspx?FileID=6787 |format=PDF |publisher=centerchem.com |access-date=3 October 2015}}</ref><ref name=bricknell>Christopher Brickell (Editor){{Google books|SrKI3yLz4ZQC|RHS Encyclopedia of Plants and Flowers (5th Edition, 2010)|page=611}}</ref><!-- also <ref name=sims/><ref name=Jekka/><ref name=Fletcher/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=Lynch/>-->

The rhizomes spread across the surface of the soil,<ref name=rhs>{{cite web|title=Iris Florentina |url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/98796/Iris-Florentina-(IB-TB)/Details |publisher=www.rhs.org.uk| access-date=1 October 2015}}</ref><ref name=irisbotanique>{{cite web |title=Chapitre I Les Iris Rhizomateux (partie 1) |url=http://irisbotanique.over-blog.com/article-chapitre-i-les-iris-rhizomateux-partie-1-123750659.html  |publisher=irisbotanique.over-blog.com |access-date=18 September 2015}}</ref><ref name=davisla>{{cite web |title=Iris germanica Florentina |date=31 May 2012 |url=https://davisla.wordpress.com/2012/05/31/plant-of-the-week-iris-germanica-florentina/ |publisher=davisla.wordpress.com |access-date=1 October 2015}}</ref> to form clumps of plants.<ref name=davisla/><ref name=shoot>{{cite web |title=Iris florentina |url=https://www.shootgardening.co.uk/plant/iris-florentina |publisher=shootgardening.co.uk |access-date=1 October 2015}}</ref> This habit can often create a dense network of fibrous roots that can crowd out other plants.<ref name=Fletcher>Neil Fletcher {{Google books|2wkdBnqQZlYC|Mediterranean Wildflowers|page=52}}</ref>

It has basal (rising up from the rhizome),<ref name=davisla/><ref name=lust>John Lust {{Google books|YsfAAwAAQBAJ|The Herb Book: The Most Complete Catalog of Herbs Ever Published (2009)|page=292}}</ref> ensiform (sword-shaped),<ref name=sims>John Sims {{Google books|JYBMAAAAYAAJ|Curtis's Botanical Magazine, Or, Flower-garden, Volume 18 (1803)|page=95}}</ref><ref name=caledonian>Caledonian Horticultural Society, Edinburgh {{Google books|cOxHAAAAYAAJ|Caledonian Horticultural Society, Edinburgh|page=245}}</ref><ref name=stefan>Stefan Buczacki {{Google books|uROWBAAAQBAJ|The Herb Bible: The definitive guide to choosing and growing herbs|page=223}}</ref><!--also <ref name=herbs/><ref name=Jekka/><ref name=Lynch/><ref name=ruth/>--> light green,<ref name=Jekka>{{cite book |last=McVicar |first=Jekka | date=2006 |edition=Revised |orig-year=1997 | title= Jekka's Complete Herb Book  | publisher=Bookmark Ltd | isbn=978-1845093709}}</ref><ref name=perennials>{{cite web |title=Iris florentina |url=http://www.perennials.com/plants/iris-florentina.html |publisher=perennials.com |access-date=1 October 2015}}</ref> pale green,<ref name=sims/> or grey-green leaves.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=davisla/><ref name=onego>{{cite web |title=Bearded Irises (IRIS) Sem. Kasatikovye |url=http://flower.onego.ru/other/iris/iris_ir.html |publisher=flower.onego.ru |access-date=5 September 2015}}</ref><!-- also <ref name=shoot/><ref name=centrechem/>-->
They are semi-evergreen,<ref name=rhs/><ref name=davisla/><ref name=shoot/> or evergreen (in mild winters).<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Stager>Walter Stager {{Google books|3-NTDKwxXpUC|Tall Bearded Iris (Fleur-de-Lis): What, When, Where, and How to Plant and subsequent plant (1917)}}</ref>{{rp|24}}
The leaves can grow up to between {{convert|30|and|70|cm|0|abbr=on}} long,<ref name=sims/><ref name=irisbotanique/> and between {{convert|2.5|and|4|cm|0|abbr=on}}wide.<ref name=Lynch>Richard Lynch and Henry Ewbank {{Google books|grvYTul5CSUC|The Book of the Iris (1904)|page=148}}</ref><ref name=davisla/> They are shorter than the stem.<ref name=sims/><ref name=caledonian/><ref name=onego/>

It has a straight,<ref name=herbs>{{cite web |title=Florentine Iris |url=http://www.herbs2000.com/herbs/herbs_florentine_iris.htm |publisher=herbs2000.com |access-date=2 October 2015}}</ref> stem or [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]], that can grow up to between {{convert|38|and|100|cm|0|abbr=on}} tall.<ref name=Jekka/><ref name=cassidy>{{cite book |last1=Cassidy |first1=George E.| last2=Linnegar | first2=Sidney | date=1987 |edition=Revised  | title= Growing Irises |location=Bromley | publisher=Christopher Helm | isbn=978-0-88192-089-5}}</ref>{{rp|63}}<ref name=hardy>William Robinson {{Google books|OqORbrG8FhAC|Hardy Flowers (1878)|page=149}}</ref><!--also<ref name=perennials/><ref name=ruth/><ref name=onego/><ref name=ClaireAustin>{{rp|142}}--> It grows to 30–60 cm tall. The leaves are grey-green, and broadly sword-shaped.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Iris Species Database<!-- Bot generated title --> |url=http://www.badbear.com/signa/signa.pl?Iris-albicans |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303182949/http://www.badbear.com/signa/signa.pl?Iris-albicans |archive-date=2016-03-03 |access-date=2007-02-18}}</ref> It may reach up to {{convert|75|-|100|cm|0|abbr=on}} after about 3 years.<ref name=stefan/> Although it may reach {{convert|121|cm|0|abbr=on}}, (in ideal conditions).<ref name=rhs/><ref name=rsland>{{cite web |title=Iris |date=13 February 2010 |url=http://rslandscapedesign.blogspot.co.uk/2010/02/hollies-new-improved-re-edited-repost.html  |publisher=rslandscapedesign.blogspot.co.uk |access-date=2 October 2015}}</ref>
The stems have 2–4 branches.<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=sims/><ref name=stebbings>{{cite book |last=Stebbings |first=Geoff |year=1997|title=The Gardener's Guide to Growing Irises |url=https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb|url-access=registration |location=Newton Abbot |publisher=David and Charles |page=[https://archive.org/details/gardenersguideto00steb/page/22 22] |isbn=978-0715305393 }}</ref> The branches reduce in size as you go up the stem,<ref name=sims/> starting from the middle.<ref name=centrechem/> The branches can be long.<ref name=stebbings/><ref name=Mathew>{{cite book |last=Mathew  |first=Brian | date=1981 | title=The Iris |url=http://historiciris.blogspot.co.uk/2009/03/iris-florentina-florentine-iris.html }}</ref>

The stem has 1–2, (scarious) membranous or sub-scarious, [[Bract#Spathe|spathes]] (leaves of the flower bud).<ref name=british>British Iris Society (1997) {{Google books|pL6uPLo7l2gC|A Guide to Species Irises: Their Identification and Cultivation|page=33}}</ref> At flowering time, the spathes become brown and papery,<ref name=Fletcher/><ref name=onego/><ref name=European>James Cullen, Sabina G. Knees, H. Suzanne Cubey (Editors) {{Google books|CkxWrDqtWLQC|The European Garden Flora Flowering Plants: A Manual for the Identification (2011) |page=340}}</ref> or fully scarious.<ref name=british/> They can be up to {{convert|40|-|80|cm|0|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Lynch/> 1.5-2 in long
The lower spathes are green and leaf-like.<ref name=sims/>

It has a short [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] (or flower stalk), and green perianth tube, that is 3.2 cm long,<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=sims/> it is covered normally by the spathes.<ref name=onego/>

The stem (and the many branches) hold between 4 and 7 flowers.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=onego/><ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|121}} at terminal ends.<ref name=European/><ref name=Dispensatory>{{Google books|hNYyAQAAMAAJ|The Dispensatory of the United States of America (1865)|page=486}}</ref> Sometimes in pairs.<ref name=herbs/><ref name=caledonian/><ref name=Dispensatory/>  The fragrant flowers,<ref name=onego/><ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|121}}<ref name=Mathew/> <!--also<ref name=davisla/><ref name=caledonian/><ref name=shoot/><ref name=rsland/><ref name=hardy/>--> smell of violets,<ref name=ruth/> appear in spring,<ref name=perennials/><ref name=hardy/><ref name=European/><!--<ref name=shoot/><ref name=perennials/>--> or early summer,<ref name=davisla/><ref name=stefan/><ref name=rsland/> or mid-summer,<ref name=Jekka/><ref name=herbs/> between late April and May,<ref name=ruth/><ref name=sims/><ref name=Stager/>{{rp|22}}<!--also<ref name=onego/><ref name=irisbotanique/>--> or between March and May.<ref Name=malta>{{cite web |title=Iris florentina |url=http://www.maltawildplants.com/IRID/Iris_florentina.php |publisher=maltawildplants.com |access-date=1 October 2015 |archive-date=6 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151006103438/http://www.maltawildplants.com/IRID/Iris_florentina.php |url-status=dead }}</ref>

The large flowers,<ref name=herbs/><ref name=perennials/><ref name="Mathew" /><ref name="European" /><ref name=Dispensatory/><!--also<ref name=ruth/>--> are up to {{convert|25|cm|0|abbr=on}} in diameter (or across).<ref name=rsland/> They come in white,<ref name=onego/><ref name=ClaireAustin>{{cite book |first=Claire |last=Austin |title=Irises; A Garden Encyclopedia |year=2005 |publisher=Timber Press |isbn=978-0881927306 }}</ref>{{rp|142}}<ref name=Gaskell>Thomas Gaskell Tuti (Editor){{Google books|v11xJgWbUDcC|Flora Europaea, Volume 5|page=89}}</ref> (sometimes described as 'dead white,<ref name=ruth/>) or greyish white,<ref name=sims/><ref name=perennials/> or bluish white,<ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|121}}<ref name=rsland/><ref name=Dispensatory/> or very pale lavender.<ref name=davisla/><ref name=stefan/> They are slightly tinged, or flushed with blue,<ref name=sims/><ref name=hardy/><ref name=European/> or pale blue,<ref name=ruth/> or lavender.<ref name=Jekka/><ref name=shoot/><ref name=Stager/>{{rp|22}} They are especially tinted when in bud.<ref name=stebbings/>

Like other irises, it has 2 pairs of petals, 3 large [[sepals]] (outer petals), known as the 'falls' and 3 inner, smaller petals (or [[tepals]]), known as the 'standards'.<ref name=Dispensatory/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|17}} The deflexed,<ref name=sims/><ref name=Dispensatory/> or drooping falls,<ref name=rhs/><ref name=centrechem/> are obovate,<ref name=onego/> or cuneate (wedge) shaped.<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=hardy/> They are {{convert|7.6|-|9|cm|0|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|3.8|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide.<ref name=Lynch/> There is some greenish-yellow veining on the haft, (section of the petal near the stem),<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Mathew/> and in the centre of the falls,<ref name=Fletcher/> there is a narrow fillet of white [[cilias]] (called a beard) with deep yellow tips,<ref name=sims/><ref name=onego/><ref name=Dispensatory/> bright yellow,<ref name=Lynch/><ref name=hardy/> or orange yellow.<ref name=irisbotanique/> <!--yellow beard<ref name=Jekka/><ref name=shoot/><ref name=rsland/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=rhs/>--> The standards are erect,<ref name=rhs/><ref name=centrechem/><ref name=sims/> oboval,<ref name=hardy/> and narrower than the falls.<ref name=onego/> The hafts of the standards, have a small white beard.<ref name=british/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|142}}

It has style branches,<ref name=centrechem/> that are toothed and 3.8 cm long, with a deltoid crests.<ref name=Lynch/>
It has an oblong shaped and pearl coloured stigma.<ref name=sims/>

After the iris has flowered, between July and August,<ref name=onego/> it produces a fusiform (spindle shaped),<ref name=onego/>  trigonal, or oblong seed capsule.<ref name=sims/>
It is longer than the seed capsule of ''Iris germanica''.<ref name=sims/> The capsule is loculicidal (has chambers),<ref name=davisla/> with 3 cells,<ref name=Dispensatory/> that hold dark brown,<ref name=onego/> or brown seeds.<ref name=centrechem/> The seeds are normally lined up like rolls of coins.<ref name=centrechem/>

===Biochemistry===
In 1973, a chemical study was carried out on Iris florentina, it found [[isoflavone]] [[glycosides]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Tsukida |first1=Kiyoshi |last2=Saiki |first2=Kayoko |last3=Ito |first3=Masayoshi  |date=September 1973 |title=New isoflavone glycosides from Iris florentina |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/256313237 |journal=Phytochemistry |volume=12 |issue=9 |pages= 2318–2319 |doi=10.1016/0031-9422(73)85153-2 |bibcode=1973PChem..12.2318T |access-date=2 October 2015}}</ref>

A 1973 study isolated a xanthone (irisxanthone) from ''Iris florentina'', which was identified as the tetraoxygenated xanthone glycoside 2-C-β-D-glucopyranosyl-5-methoxy-1,3,6-trihydroxyxanthone<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Arisawa|first1=Munehisa |last2=Morita|first2=Naokata|last3= Kondo |first3=Yoshikazu |last4=Takemoto |first4=Tsunematsu|date=1973|title=The constituents of ''Iris florentina'' L.(3). Structure of irisxanthone, a new C-glycosylxanthone |journal=Chem. Pharm. Bull. |volume= 21|issue=11 |pages= 2562–2565 |doi=10.1248/CPB.21.2562 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

In 2014, a study was carried out on the essential oil of ''Iris florentina''. It found several compounds including [[decanoic acid]], [[ethanon]],{{typo help inline|date=December 2020}} α-iron, trans-2,6-γ-iron, [[lauric acid]], [[myristic acid]], [[palmitic acid]], 9,12 oktadecadienoic acid and hexanedioic acid bis ester.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kara |first1=Nimet |last2=Baydar |first2=Hasan |date=2014 |title=Scent Components In Essential Oil, Resinoids And Absolute Of Iris (Iris florentina L.) |url=http://dergi.omu.edu.tr/omuanajas/article/view/1009002793 |journal=Anadolu Journal of Agricultural Sciences |volume=29 |issue=1 |pages=70 |doi=10.7161/anajas.2014.29.1.70 |access-date=1 October 2015 |doi-access=free |archive-date=6 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151006092714/http://dergi.omu.edu.tr/omuanajas/article/view/1009002793 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In 2015, a study was carried out on the antioxidant and anticholinesterase potential of the iris.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ullaha |first1=Farhat |last2=Ayaza |first2=Muhammad |last3=Sadiqa |first3=Abdul |last4=Hussaina |first4=Abid |last5=Ahmada |first5=Sajjad |last6=Imrana |first6=Muhammad |last7=Zeba |first7=Anwar |date=21 April 2015 |title=Phenolic, flavonoid contents, anticholinesterase and antioxidant evaluation of Iris germanica var; florentina |url=https://figshare.com/ndownloader/files/2172440 |journal=Natural Product Research |volume=30 |issue=12 |pages=1440–1444 |doi=10.1080/14786419.2015.1057585 |pmid=26166432 |s2cid=20384953|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

===Karyology===
As most irises are [[diploid]], having two sets of [[chromosomes]], this can be used to identify hybrids and classification of groupings.<ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|18}}
''Iris florentina'' has a count of 2n=44, meaning it is a [[tetraploid]].<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref>{{cite journal |last1= Twardovska |first1=M.O. |last2=Andreev |first2=I.O. |last3=Kunakh |first3=V.A. |title=Karyotypes of species of the genus Iris from the flora of Ukraine |journal=Vascular Plants: Taxonomy, Geography and Floristics |volume= 71|issue= 5|pages= 581–589|doi=10.15407/ukrbotj71.05.581 |year=2014 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
[[File:Iris florentina Sydenham Edwards.jpg|thumb|Painted illustration of Iris florentina by [[Sydenham Edwards]] for [[Curtis's Botanical Magazine]] in 1803]]
It has the common names of 'Florentine Iris',<ref name=rhs/><ref name=davisla/><ref name=caledonian/><!--also<ref name=herbs/><ref name=shoot/><ref name=lust/>--> 'Florentine Flag' (in the US),<ref name=sims/> 'Glaive lily',<ref name=rhs/><ref name=shoot/> 'White German Iris',<ref name=Fletcher/> and 'White Flower De Luce',<ref name=herbs/>

It is sometimes known as ''orris root'', which also comes from the rhizomes of ''Iris germanica'' and ''Iris pallida''.<ref name=herbs/>

The French call it commonly as 'la flambe blanche' (the white torch of the garden).<ref name=Stager/>{{rp|20}}<ref name=Helvey>Jennifer Helvey{{Google books|LUZ-dHerY3sC|Irises: Vincent Van Gogh in the Garden|page=29}}</ref>

It is known in [[Malta]] as 'Fjurduliz abjad',<ref Name=malta/> in Danish as 'violrod', in France as 'Iris de florence', in German as 'Florentinische Schwertlilie', in Spanish (and Portuguese) as  'lirio blanco' or 'lirio de Florencia'.<ref>John H. Wiersema and Blanca León{{Google books|AIrNBQAAQBAJ|World Economic Plants: A Standard Reference, Second Edition|page=370}}</ref>

The Latin [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''florentina'' refers to a 'Latinised' word meaning ‘from Florence’.<ref name=davisla/><ref name=Stager/>{{rp|22}}<ref>D. Gledhill {{Google books|NJ6PyhVuecwC|The Names of Plants|page=176}}</ref>

It was first collected in Italy, and then introduced to N. Europe in about 1500.<ref name=cornell>{{cite book |last=Sand |first=Austin W.W. | date=July 1926  | title=Cornell Memoir, 100 Study of Pogoniris Varieties |url= http://historiciris.blogspot.co.uk/2009/03/iris-florentina-florentine-iris.html }}</ref><ref name=american>{{cite web  |first=Pries |last=Bob |title=(SPEC) Iris florentina L. |date=12 December 2014 |url=http://wiki.irises.org/bin/view/Spec/SpecFlorentina |publisher=wiki.irises.org (American Iris Society)| access-date=1 October 2015}}</ref>
It has been cultivated for centuries in Europe.<ref name=Fletcher/>

It was first published and described by [[Carl Linnaeus]], in [[Systema Naturae]] Edition 10, Issue2 on page863 on 7 June 1759, as ''Iris florentina''.<ref name=ipni>{{cite book |title=Iridaceae Iris florentina L. |volume=2 |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=438598-1 |publisher=ipni.org (International Plant Names Index) |access-date=2 October 2015}}</ref><ref name=grin>{{GRIN | ''Iris florentina'' | 400617 | accessdate=1 October 2015}}</ref> It was thought to be similar to ''Iris germanica'', but with white flowers.<ref name=Mathew/>

In 1796, ''Iris officinalis'' Salisb. was published by [[Richard Anthony Salisbury|Salisb]] in Prodr. Stirp. Chap. Allerton Vol.43.<ref>{{cite book |title=Iridaceae Iris officinalis Salisb. |url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=438928-1 |publisher=ipni.org (International Plant Names Index) |access-date=2 October 2015}}</ref> But this was later classed as ''Iris florentina''.

In 1910, [[William Rickatson Dykes]] in [[The Gardeners' Chronicle]] of September 17, 1910,<ref name=Mathew/>  felt that ''Iris florentina'' was not a wild species but had hybrid origin,<ref name=onego/> or form of ''Iris germanica''.<ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|121}}

In his book, 'The Iris' in 1981, [[Brian Mathew]], re-classified the iris as ''Iris germanica'' 'Florentina'.<ref name=Mathew/><ref name=European/><ref name=american/>

This later became ''Iris germanica'' nothovar. ''florentina''.

It was verified by [[United States Department of Agriculture]] and the [[Agricultural Research Service]] on 19 October 1994, then updated on 12 September 2005, as ''Iris germanica'' L. nothovar. ''florentina'' Dykes.<ref name=grin/>

It is listed in the [[Encyclopedia of Life]] as ''Iris germanica var. florentina''.<ref name=eol>{{cite web |title=Iris germanica var. florentina |url= http://eol.org/pages/1263356/overview |publisher=eol.org |access-date=2 October 2015}}</ref>

''Iris florentina'' is an accepted name by the [[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS]],<ref name=rhs/> it was given the [[Award of Garden Merit]] in 1994.<ref name=bricknell/><ref name=davisla/><ref name=shoot/>

==Distribution and habitat==
It is [[native plant|native]] to central,<ref name=Lynch/> and southern Europe.<ref name=ruth/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=Stager/>{{rp|24}}

===Range===
It is found in Italy,<ref name=hardy/><ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|142}}<ref name=Annals>{{cite web |title=Annals of Horticulture and Year book of Information on Practical Gardening for 1847 |url=http://www.forgottenbooks.com/readbook_text/The_Annals_of_Horticulture_and_Year-Book_of_Information_on_Practical_1000024173/137 |publisher=forgottenbooks.com |access-date=2 October 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151006154449/http://www.forgottenbooks.com/readbook_text/The_Annals_of_Horticulture_and_Year-Book_of_Information_on_Practical_1000024173/137 |archive-date=6 October 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref><!--also <ref name=Dispensatory/><ref name=sims/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=centrechem/>--> (including [[Tuscany]],<ref name=stebbings/>) France,<ref name=centrechem/><ref name=cornell/> and the Mediterranean islands,<ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|121}}<ref name=ClaireAustin/>{{rp|142}} (including [[Malta]]).<ref name=malta/> 

''Iris florentina'' has been cultivated since ancient times and may be the oldest iris in cultivation. Collected by [[Johan Martin Christian Lange|Lange]] in 1860, it has been in cultivation since at least 1400 BC. Originating from [[Yemen]] and [[Saudi Arabia]], it appears in a wall painting of the [[Botanical Garden]] of [[Tuthmosis III]] in the [[Temple of Amun]] at [[Karnak]] in ancient [[Thebes (Egypt)|Thebes]] dated around 1426 BC.

Botanist [[René Louiche Desfontaines|Desfontaines]] found it in [[Algiers]], where it is grown with ''Iris germanica'' near graves.<ref name=sims/>

It has been naturalised in many other countries, from the Mediterranean,<ref name=ruth/> (including west Africa and southern [[Spain]],<ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|121}}) to [[India]],<ref name=irisbotanique/> and [[Iran]].<ref name=herbs/> In Russia, it grows in the south of western [[Siberia]]. Outside of Russia, it is found in [[Kazakhstan]], [[Mongolia]] and [[China]].<ref name=onego/> 
 
In many regions of the world, especially in Italy, it is cultivated for commercial use.<ref name=herbs/><ref name=lust/>

===Habitat===
It grows on sunny mountain slopes,<ref name=herbs/> on [[steppes]], sandy or rocky dry slopes.<ref name=onego/>

It naturalises along roadsides, field margins, olive groves, abandoned vineyards and other cultivated sites.<ref name=Fletcher/>

==Conservation==
All the stations in the other countries where it has become naturalized for centuries, it is gone, or they are declining.<ref name=irisbotanique/>
Not protected by law and not listed in the flora section of the National Red Data book (1989)<ref name=malta/>

==Cultivation==
It is [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]],<ref name=sims/> to between [[USDA]] Zone 3 and Zone 9,<ref name=davisla/> or between 5 and 8.<ref name=rsland/>
It is also hardy to Zone H2 (in Europe),<ref name=European/> between −15 and -20oC (5 to −4oF).<ref>{{cite web |title=Plant Hardiness |url=http://theseedsite.co.uk/hardiness.html |publisher=theseedsite.co |access-date=3 August 2015}}</ref> It has been tested for hardiness in Russia, in the botanical gardens of; [[Barnaul]], [[Novosibirsk]], [[St. Petersburg]] and [[Ufa]].<ref name=onego/> In the winter, it requires protection from moisture (in Russia).<ref name=onego/>
It can be cultivated well throughout Europe and N America, except in the warm moist climates of Florida and Gulf Coast.<ref name=Jekka/>

''Iris florentina'' is included in the [[Tasmania Fire Service]]'s list of low [[flammability]] plants, indicating that it is suitable for growing within a building protection zone.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Iris Species Database<!-- Bot generated title --> |url=http://www.badbear.com/signa/signa.pl?Iris-albicans |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303182949/http://www.badbear.com/signa/signa.pl?Iris-albicans |archive-date=2016-03-03 |access-date=2007-02-18}}</ref>

It prefers to grow in moist, well drained soils,<ref name="rhs" /><ref name="davisla" /><ref name="rsland" /><!--also<ref name=perennials/>--> in [[loam]].<ref name="rhs" /><ref name="perennials" /> It can tolerate sandy soils,<ref name="perennials" /> or any common garden soil.<ref name="caledonian" /><ref name="hardy" />
It also tolerates most soil [[pH|pH levels]] of, and will tolerate very alkali or acid soils.<ref name="rhs" /><ref name="davisla" /><ref name="perennials" />

It prefers a situation in full sun,<ref name=rhs/><ref name=perennials/><ref name=rsland/> to light shade.<ref name=davisla/>

It will suffer from rhizome viruses in waterlogged soil.<ref name=rhs/><ref name=onego/>

It can be grown in mixed flower borders,<ref name=rhs/><ref name=perennials/> rock gardens,<ref name=onego/> and beside the edges of shrubberies.<ref name=hardy/> As well as being [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in the garden.<ref>William Robinson {{Google books|xllfANqStZwC|The Wild Garden: Expanded Edition|page=267}}</ref>
It can be a cut flower for displays.<ref name=perennials/>

It is deer and rabbit resistant,<ref name=perennials/> but can suffer from [[leaf spot]],<ref name=rhs/> [[Iris borer]],<ref name=perennials/> [[thrips]],<ref name=rhs/> slug and snails.<ref name=rhs/><ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=stefan/>
[[Aphid]]s ''[[Aphis newtoni]]'' and  ''[[Dysaphis tulipae]]'' can also be found on the plant.<ref>R. L. Blackman, Victor F. Eastop {{Google books|UZqkLr9m4GUC|Aphids on the World's Herbaceous Plants and Shrubs|page=553}}</ref>

The irises are planted shallow, leaving the tops of the rhizomes exposed,<ref name=rsland/> to the sun. They are not mulched, as this could cause rotting to the rhizomes.<ref name=stefan/> They can be fertilized in early spring, and again in late summer,<ref name=perennials/> with a general fertilizer or [[bone meal]].<ref name=stefan/>
The foliage can be cut back in the autumn, after the flowers have faded.<ref name=rhs/><ref name=stefan/>

===Propagation===
''Iris florentina'' can only be propagated by [[Division (horticulture)|division]],<ref name=caledonian/><ref name=onego/><ref name=hardy/> of the rhizomes,<ref name=herbs/> after flowering,<ref name=rsland/><ref name=stebbings/> up to six weeks after flowering,<ref name=davisla/> and in the autumn.<ref name=rhs/><ref name=sims/>

They should be divided every 3 to 4 years,<ref name=perennials/><ref name=rsland/> when large clumps.<ref name=davisla/>

The old woody-like centre, should be removed,<ref name=stefan/><ref name=rsland/> along with any damaged sections.<ref name=ruth/> The rhizomes are then left exposed, to allow the cuts to [[callus]], then the foliage is trimmed,<ref name=ruth/> (to reduce water loss). Then the new rhizome sections can be re-planted, in new situations and at a shallow depth.<ref name=stefan/>

===Hybrids and cultivars===
It has a few cultivars including; 'Alba',<ref name=cornell/> 'Blue Zua',<ref name=american/> 'Bluzugraf',<ref name=american/> 'Elizabeth Huntington',<ref name=american/> 'Elsie Crouch Diltz',<ref name=american/> 'Firmament',<ref name=american/> 'Florentina purpurea',<ref name=american/> 'Gambetta',<ref name=cornell/> 'Janet Barnes',<ref name=american/> 'New Orleans' (which has light grey flowers),<ref name=Annals/> 'Queen Emma',<ref name=cornell/> 'Silver King',<ref name=cornell/> and 'Zua'.<ref name=american/>

There are a few crosses: 'Altar Candles', 'Tan Crown', 'Vendor'.<ref name=american/>

==Toxicity==
[[File:Iris germanica florentina - Köhler–s Medizinal-Pflanzen-078.jpg|thumb|An 1897 botanical image from [[Köhler's Medizinal-Pflanzen]] ]]

Like many other irises, most parts of the plant are poisonous (rhizome and leaves) and, if ingested, can cause stomach pains and vomiting.<ref name=irisbotanique/><ref name=shoot/><ref name=perennials/> Also, handling the plant may cause a skin irritation or an allergic reaction.<ref>David G Spoerke and Susan C. Smolinske{{Google books|a7-f66fRfzQC|Toxicity of Houseplants|page=236}}</ref>

It was noted by G.R Winter (in 1948, J Periodont 19:108) that allergic manifestations can be caused by the use of a dentifrice (teeth cleaner) containing orris root powder.<ref>D. Jesse Wagstaff {{Google books|h7tbd-5ZAQ8C|International Poisonous Plants Checklist: An Evidence-Based Reference|page=207}}</ref>

==Uses==
{{Main|Orris root}}
The violet scented rhizome has many uses including, a perfume,<ref name=caledonian/> for mixing with hair powder,<ref name=sims/><ref name=caledonian/> powder used for washing clothes, hair, and teeth,<ref name=Joanne/> used as a fresh scent for linen, a base for dry shampoos, base for tooth powders, in face-packs, as a [[fixative (perfumery)|fixative]] in [[pot-pourri]].<ref name=Jekka/>

It was used medicinally as an [[expectorant]] (clearance of mucus from the airways) and [[decongestant]].<ref name=Annals/><ref name=Joanne/> It was also formerly used for treating wounds and chest infections.<ref name=Fletcher/> It was also administered for the cure of [[dropsy]].<ref name=Medical>John Stephenson and James Morss Churchill{{Google books|54IfAAAAYAAJ|Medical Botany, Or, Illustrations and Descriptions of the medicinal, Volume 1 (1831)|page=217}}</ref> It was also used sometimes for bronchitis, coughs and sore throat, for colic and for congestion of the liver.<ref name=lust/> It is rarely used medicinally nowadays.<ref name=Jekka/>
It has been chewed as a breath freshener, carved into rosary beads, and given to babies as a teething aid.<ref name=Joanne/>

It is still used in cosmetics,<ref name=stefan/> perfumes, soaps and sweets. Also it is used for maturing [[Chianti]] wine,<ref name=davisla/><ref name=stebbings/> and as an ingredient in [[Bombay Sapphire]] [[Gin]].<ref>Patrick Bowe and Michael D. DeHart {{Google books|cQuEjqSnnNYC|Gardens and Plants of the Getty Villa|page=154}}</ref>

==Culture==
''Iris florentina'' is considered one of the irises (with ''Iris pseudacorus'') that inspired the [[fleur-de-lys]] (or fleur-de-luce) of heraldry,<ref name=Jekka/><ref name=herbs/><ref name=stefan/> which was the symbol of the city of Florence for centuries,<ref name=herbs/><ref name=irisbotanique/> and is on the [[coat of arms]] of the city.

A legend of the city tells that on [[Saint Reparata|St. Reparata's Day]] in the year 405 the Goths had the city of Florence under siege, and the city defences were failing. Suddenly, St. Reparata appeared in the midst of the fighting, holding a blood-red banner emblazoned with a white iris. This changed the battle and lifted the spirits of the Florentines, which led them to be victorious. In gratitude (to St Reparata), the city adopted the symbol for its coat of arms<ref name=Joanne>{{cite web |first=Joanne |last=O'Sullivan | title=Consider the iris, A look at Florence's best-known symbol |date=21 April 2011 |url=http://www.theflorentine.net/articles/article-view.asp?issuetocId=6830 |publisher=theflorentine.net |access-date=3 October 2015}}</ref> from the eleventh century onwards.<ref name=Giglio>{{cite web |first=Liesbeth |last=Hogerbrugge |title=The history of the Giglio of Florence |date=16 August 2013 |url=http://www.intoflorence.com/history-giglio-florence/ |publisher=intoflorence.com |access-date=3 October 2015}}</ref> After the battle in which the [[Guelfs]] (or Guelphs) routed the [[Ghibellines]] in the late thirteenth century,<ref name=Joanne/><ref name=Giglio/><ref name=nzz>{{cite news |first=Gabriele |last=Detterer |title=As the Irises in the field |date=14 April 2002 |url=http://www.nzz.ch/article82V83-1.385530 |access-date=3 October 2015|newspaper=[[Neue Zürcher Zeitung]] }}</ref> the colours were reversed, and the red lily (or red giglio,<ref name=Giglio/>) on a field of white became the symbol of Florence.<ref name=Joanne/><ref name=Giglio/><ref>{{cite web |title=The Florentine Iris, History of a symbol |date=25 May 2015 |url=http://www.florencewithguide.com/blog/the-florentine-iris/ |publisher=florencewithguide.com |access-date=3 October 2015}}</ref>

During the Middle Ages and the [[Renaissance period]], ‘Iris green' (or 'Verdelis' and 'Vert d'iris'),<ref name=sims/> was a rare, paint pigment colour used by [[manuscript]] illuminators and painters.<ref name=Joanne/><ref name=Thompson>Daniel V. Thompson {{Google books|MU68AQAAQBAJ|The Materials and Techniques of Medieval Painting (2012)|page=171}}</ref> It was made from the juice of the fresh flowers of ''Iris florentine'' and/or ''Iris germanica''.<ref name=sims/><ref name=Thompson/><ref name=Firenze>{{cite web |title=Report of the 1st International Symposium on Iris – Florence | date=14 May 1963 |url=http://historiciris.blogspot.co.uk/2009/03/iris-florentina-florentine-iris.html |publisher=historiciris.blogspot.co.uk |access-date=2 October 2015}}</ref> The bluish or purplish petal juice was steeped (soaked) in boiling water, then combined and thickened with [[alum]].<ref name=Joanne/><ref name=Thompson/> It then produces a clear green paint. It was used in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. It can not be distinguished from 'sap green' (or 'verte de vessie' or 'verde di vesica') a paint juice derived from Buckthorn berries.<ref name=Thompson/>

On the [[triptych]] painting, "Adorazione dei Pastori" by painter [[Hugo van der Goes]] (in 1475 or 1476), it has images of ''Iris florentina'' and ''Iris pallida''.<ref name=cassidy/>{{rp|20}}<ref name=nzz/> It is in the Botticelli room of the [[Uffizi|Uffizi Gallery]].<ref name=nzz/>

The white flowers of ''Iris florentina'' are also used church decoration,<ref name=Stager/>{{rp|20}} and planted around graves in the city of Florence, as a token of respect to the deceased.<ref name=Helvey/><ref>Sir Joseph Paxton (Editor){{Google books|0GcCAAAAYAAJ|Paxton's Magazine of Botany, and Register of Flowering Plants, Volume 1 |page=83}}</ref>
